title: Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls, or Both? How to Choose Your Uganda Savannah Park
meta_title: Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls: Which Suits You Best
meta_description: Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls compared: wildlife, boat trips, drive times and UWA fees, so you can pick the right Uganda park or plan both.
excerpt: Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls compared on wildlife, boat trips, distance from Kampala and official UWA fees, with clear advice on which Uganda park fits your route.
content:
Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls is the choice most Uganda safari planners face, and the short answer is this: pick Murchison Falls for giraffes, big herds, the Nile and the falls, and pick Queen Elizabeth for tree-climbing lions, the Kazinga Channel and an easy link to Bwindi's gorillas. With 8 days or more, do both.

Both parks are savannah reserves with lions, elephants, buffaloes and hippos, so brochures make them sound alike. On the ground they feel very different, sit at opposite ends of the country and fit different routes. This guide compares them side by side with distances, official fees and honest trade-offs, so you can settle Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls for your own Uganda safari itinerary.

Quick Facts

  • Murchison Falls size: 3,840 km², Uganda's largest national park
  • Queen Elizabeth size: 1,978 km², between Lake Edward and Lake George
  • From Kampala: Murchison about 305 km (4-5 hours to the southern gate); Queen Elizabeth about 410 km (7-8 hours)
  • Entry fee (foreign non-resident): US$45 Murchison, US$40 Queen Elizabeth per day (UWA, checked November 2026)
  • Signature sights: Murchison: the falls, Nile launch, giraffes, shoebill. Queen Elizabeth: Kazinga Channel, Ishasha lions, Kyambura chimps
  • Driest months: December to February and June to September

Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls at a glance

In any Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls comparison, Murchison is the bigger, wilder northern park built around the Nile, while Queen Elizabeth is the more varied southwestern park built around lakes, craters and a channel. The table sets them side by side.

PointMurchison FallsQueen Elizabeth
LocationNorth-west, along the Victoria Nile above Lake AlbertSouth-west, on the equator below the Rwenzori region
Size3,840 km²1,978 km²
LandscapeRolling grassland, borassus palms, river gorgeOpen plains, crater lakes, papyrus swamp, forest gorge
Big drawsThe falls, Nile launch, Nubian giraffes, Uganda kob herdsKazinga Channel cruise, Ishasha lions, Kyambura chimps
Mammals and birds (UWA)144 mammal and 556 bird speciesOver 95 mammal and 600+ bird species
Fits best withZiwa rhinos, Budongo chimps, a short trip from KampalaKibale chimps, Bwindi gorillas, Lake Mburo

Both figures above come from the Uganda Wildlife Authority's own Murchison Falls park page and Queen Elizabeth park page. One point the Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls debate often misses: neither park has rhinos. The nearest are at Ziwa Rhino Sanctuary on the road north, so Murchison trips often stop there.

Which park has better wildlife?

On wildlife, Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls splits cleanly: Murchison has the denser herds and the giraffes, Queen Elizabeth the better predator and primate variety. Count animals in view and Murchison wins; want lions in trees and chimpanzees in one park, and Queen Elizabeth does.

Murchison Falls: herds, giraffes and the Buligi grasslands

The game drives in Murchison take place north of the Nile, on the grassland tracks of the Buligi area towards the Lake Albert delta. UWA counts about 35,000 Uganda kobs, over 10,000 buffaloes and more than 900 elephants in the park. Giraffes live only in this northern sector, and lions follow the kob herds across the open plains.

Mornings bring long views over palm-dotted grassland. Leopards are seen along the riverine bush, mostly at dawn and dusk. Where Murchison loses the Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls contest is primates: for chimpanzees you add Budongo Forest on the drive in.

Queen Elizabeth: Kasenyi lions, Ishasha and Kyambura Gorge

Queen Elizabeth packs more habitats into a smaller area. The Kasenyi plains in the north are the morning game drive, with Uganda kobs, buffaloes, elephants and the lions that hunt them. Ishasha, the southern sector, is the place for lions resting in fig trees, and Kyambura Gorge is a sunken strip of forest with a habituated chimpanzee community.

The catch is that Ishasha is a long drive from the Mweya and Kasenyi area, so most travellers see it in passing on the way south to Bwindi. If tree-climbing lions decide Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls for you, plan a night near Ishasha rather than a quick detour. What are the boat trips like in each park?

Boat trips are where Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls is closest to a draw. The Murchison launch heads upstream on the Nile to the foot of the falls; the Queen Elizabeth cruise runs along the Kazinga Channel between two lakes. UWA charges foreign non-residents US$30 for each (checked November 2026).

The Nile launch and the delta in Murchison

The launch from Paraa travels about 17 km upstream and takes roughly two hours, according to the UWA conservation tariff for January 2027 to June 2028. Hippos, crocodiles and elephants line the banks, and the trip ends below the white water where the Nile forces through a narrow rock gap and drops about 45 metres. Go to the top of the falls as well: the noise and spray up close are a different experience.

Downstream, boats head into the papyrus of the Lake Albert delta, where the shoebill is most often seen. BirdLife International lists the park as an Important Bird Area, and keen birders often rate the delta above anything in Queen Elizabeth for that one bird.

The Kazinga Channel cruise

The Kazinga Channel is a 40 km waterway linking Lake Edward and Lake George, and the two-hour afternoon cruise from Mweya keeps close to the shore. It is one of the best places in Uganda to watch hippos at close range, with buffaloes and elephants coming down to drink and huge numbers of water birds. For photographers weighing Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls, it is the easier cruise, since the boat stays near the bank the whole time.

Which is easier to reach from Kampala or Entebbe?

Distance settles Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls for many short trips. Murchison is the easier park to reach by road, about 305 km and 4-5 hours from Kampala to the southern gate. Queen Elizabeth is about 410 km away and takes at least 7-8 hours, so it rarely works as a quick trip unless you fly.

Those times come from UWA and match what we plan around, though Kampala traffic can add an hour leaving the city. From Murchison's gate, allow another hour or two to most lodges, and remember that game drives happen across the river, so a morning starts with the crossing at Paraa. In Queen Elizabeth, the Mweya peninsula puts you within reach of both the Kasenyi plains and the channel.

Flying in

Scheduled and charter flights from Entebbe or Kajjansi serve Pakuba airstrip for Murchison, and Kasese, Mweya or Kihihi (for Ishasha) for Queen Elizabeth. Flying changes the Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls maths, saving a full day each way on the Queen Elizabeth side, and makes most sense when you are also heading to Bwindi. See our fly-in safari options if road time is your main worry.

What does each park cost to visit?

On fees, Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls is nearly even: Queen Elizabeth is US$5 a day cheaper to enter, but activities change the total. Below are UWA's foreign non-resident adult rates from the 2024-2026 tariff, still on the UWA site, and the January 2027 revision (checked November 2026).

Fee (foreign non-resident adult)Current UWA tariffFrom January 2027
Murchison Falls park entry, per dayUS$45US$45
Queen Elizabeth park entry, per dayUS$40US$40
Launch trip (Nile to the falls, or Kazinga Channel)US$30US$30
Chimpanzee tracking, Kyambura GorgeUS$100US$240
Lion tracking experience, Queen ElizabethUS$200US$500
Guide for a game drive in your own vehicleUS$25US$30

Children aged 5 and over pay reduced entry (US$25 in Murchison and US$20 in Queen Elizabeth on the 2027 tariff). Fees change without much notice in Uganda, so confirm current rates with UWA or with us before you pay a deposit. Lodges in both parks range from simple rest camps to river- and lake-view lodges, so accommodation rarely decides Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls.

Which park suits your trip?

Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls depends less on which park is better and more on what else is on your list. Most of our Uganda trips are built around gorillas, and that one fact pushes many travellers towards Queen Elizabeth, while those with a short window or a love of big open landscapes lean to Murchison.

Choose Murchison Falls if

  • You have three or four days and want a full safari without a long drive.
  • Giraffes, big kob herds and the falls matter more to you than primates.
  • You want rhino tracking at Ziwa on the way, and shoebill in the delta.

Choose Queen Elizabeth if

  • Gorilla trekking is the main event, since the park sits on the road between Kibale and Bwindi.
  • You want lions in fig trees at Ishasha, or chimpanzees in Kyambura Gorge.
  • A relaxed boat-based safari suits you or your family better than long game drives.
  • You are adding chimpanzee trekking in Kibale to the same trip.

Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls when you can do both

With 8-10 days, the best answer to Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls is both, running north to south: Murchison first, then Kibale, Queen Elizabeth and finally Bwindi. UWA puts the drive from Murchison to Fort Portal at 280 km and at least 6 hours, so a night in Kibale breaks the journey neatly. Groups can follow the same loop on our 9-day Uganda gorilla safari for clubs, and our Bwindi gorilla trekking guide covers the final leg.

When is the best time to visit each park?

The drier months, December to February and June to September, are the best time for both parks, with shorter grass, firmer tracks and animals gathering near water. The wetter spells, roughly March to May and October to November, bring fewer vehicles but slower, muddier drives.

Murchison's northern bank gets hot in January and February, so game drives start early and the midday launch can feel sticky. Queen Elizabeth sits higher, mostly between about 910 and 1,350 m on UWA's figures, and feels a little milder. Season rarely changes the Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls decision, though rain affects Ishasha's tracks more than the Kasenyi plains. For a month-specific plan, see our Uganda in January guide, or compare the whole country with Kenya in our Kenya vs Uganda safari comparison.

MonthsMurchison FallsQueen Elizabeth
December to FebruaryDry, hot afternoons, excellent drivesDry, good for Ishasha and Kasenyi
March to MayLong rains, lush grass, some tracks slowWet, cruise still runs, Ishasha tracks harder
June to SeptemberDry, cooler, peak seasonDry, peak season, best for combining with Bwindi
October to NovemberShort rains, green and quieterShort rains, fewer vehicles

Insider Tips

  • Do the top of the falls: Whichever way Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls goes, if Murchison is in, see the falls from above too, not just from the launch.
  • Book the morning crossing early: In Murchison the game drive starts across the Nile at Paraa, so an early crossing means more time on the grassland before the heat.
  • Sit on the shore side: On the Kazinga cruise, ask for a seat facing the bank where the boat runs closest.
  • Plan Ishasha as a night: A rushed detour on the way to Bwindi often misses the lions; one night nearby gives you a second chance.
  • Watch the 2027 fees: Kyambura chimp tracking and lion tracking rise sharply in January 2027, so book early-2027 activities with the new prices in mind.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Queen Elizabeth or Murchison Falls better for a first Uganda safari?

For a first Uganda safari, Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls usually comes down to the rest of the route. Queen Elizabeth sits on the way to Bwindi, so it suits a gorilla trip with no extra driving. Murchison Falls is the better single savannah park, with giraffes, bigger herds and the falls themselves, and it is closer to Kampala.

Are there giraffes in Queen Elizabeth National Park?

No. Queen Elizabeth National Park has no giraffes and no zebras, which surprises many visitors. In Uganda you see giraffes in Murchison Falls (north of the Nile), Kidepo Valley and Lake Mburo. If giraffes matter to you, Murchison Falls is the park to choose, or add Lake Mburo on the way to Bwindi.

How many days do you need in Murchison Falls and Queen Elizabeth?

Two nights in each park is the comfortable minimum. Murchison Falls needs one morning game drive north of the Nile, one afternoon launch to the falls and time at the top of the falls. Queen Elizabeth needs a Kasenyi morning drive and a Kazinga Channel cruise, plus a third night if you want Ishasha or Kyambura Gorge.

Can you see tree-climbing lions in Murchison Falls?

Tree-climbing lions are linked to the Ishasha sector in the south of Queen Elizabeth National Park, where lions rest in fig trees. Murchison Falls has lions on the open grassland north of the Nile, but climbing behaviour is not what the park is known for. Sightings in Ishasha are never guaranteed either.

Which park is cheaper, Murchison Falls or Queen Elizabeth?

Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls on price is close. Queen Elizabeth is slightly cheaper to enter: UWA charges foreign non-residents US$40 per day there against US$45 in Murchison Falls (checked November 2026). Launch trips cost the same in both. The bigger cost difference is transport: Murchison is a shorter drive from Kampala, while Queen Elizabeth is cheaper when combined with Bwindi.

Final Thoughts

Murchison Falls gives you the Nile, the falls and the fuller savannah; Queen Elizabeth gives you the channel, the Ishasha lions and the shortest path to Bwindi. With a few days, let that settle Queen Elizabeth vs Murchison Falls; with a week, link them.
